questions.q: A Glue ETL job reads from an RDS MySQL database. Security requires the password to change every 30 days with no failed connections during rotation. Which approach fits?

options.t: Secrets Manager with Lambda rotation using the single-user strategy
options.why: Wrong: the same user's password changes, so open connections with the old password can fail briefly.

options.t: Secrets Manager with Lambda rotation using the alternating-users strategy
options.why: Right: two users are rotated in turn, so one credential is always valid and there is no downtime window.

options.t: Parameter Store SecureString with an EventBridge reminder
options.why: Wrong: Parameter Store has no built-in rotation and a reminder does not change the credential.

options.t: A Lambda environment variable updated by hand every 30 days
options.why: Wrong: manual, visible in configuration, and not rotated in the database.

questions.explain: Zero-downtime database rotation uses alternating users.
questions.remember: Rotation with no downtime → Secrets Manager Lambda rotation with the alternating-users (two-user) strategy. Single-user is simpler but can break open connections.
variants: Rotation is fine with a brief failure window → single-user strategy.
The database is an RDS/Aurora master user → managed rotation, no Lambda.
Credential does not need rotating, only config → Parameter Store.

questions.q: A team creates an Aurora cluster and wants nobody to ever see or handle the admin password, with automatic rotation and no rotation Lambda to maintain. What should they do?

options.t: Create the cluster with `ManageMasterUserPassword` enabled
options.why: Right: the service creates the master secret in Secrets Manager and rotates it with managed rotation, so no Lambda is needed.

options.t: Store the password in Parameter Store as a SecureString
options.why: Wrong: no rotation, and someone still has to know the password.

options.t: Create a custom secret and attach the rotation Lambda template
options.why: Wrong: works, but it needs a Lambda you maintain and the password is still handled by people.

options.t: Hard-code the password in the application and rotate on deploy
options.why: Wrong: hard-coded credentials are exactly what Secrets Manager removes.

questions.explain: Managed master user secrets are created and rotated by the database service.
questions.remember: RDS/Aurora/Redshift/DocumentDB admin password with no handling and no Lambda → ManageMasterUserPassword (managed secret, managed rotation).
variants: Application user (not master) credentials → custom secret with Lambda rotation.
No stored password at all → IAM database authentication.
Redshift admin → same managed master user secret option.

questions.q: A rotation Lambda for an RDS database in private subnets times out on the `setSecret` and `createSecret` steps. What is the most likely fix?

options.t: Increase the secret's recovery window
options.why: Wrong: the recovery window only applies to deletion.

options.t: Place the Lambda in the database's VPC and give it a Secrets Manager VPC endpoint or NAT
options.why: Right: the Lambda must reach both the database and the Secrets Manager API.

options.t: Switch the KMS key to `aws/secretsmanager`
options.why: Wrong: the key type does not cause network timeouts.

options.t: Enable multi-Region replication
options.why: Wrong: replication does not give the Lambda network paths.

questions.explain: The rotation Lambda needs network access to the DB and to Secrets Manager.
questions.remember: Rotation timeouts → check networking: same VPC/subnets/security groups as the DB, plus a Secrets Manager VPC endpoint or NAT.
variants: AccessDenied in the rotation Lambda → fix its execution role (GetSecretValue, PutSecretValue, UpdateSecretVersionStage, KMS).
Secrets Manager cannot invoke the Lambda → add the resource policy for secretsmanager.amazonaws.com.
Rotation stuck on AWSPENDING → fix and re-run, or CancelRotateSecret.

questions.q: During rotation, which staging label marks the new version before it becomes the version returned by default, and which step promotes it?

options.t: `AWSPENDING`, promoted by `finishSecret`
options.why: Right: createSecret labels the new version AWSPENDING and finishSecret moves AWSCURRENT to it, making the old one AWSPREVIOUS.

options.t: `AWSPREVIOUS`, promoted by `createSecret`
options.why: Wrong: AWSPREVIOUS is the last current version, not the new one.

options.t: `AWSCURRENT`, promoted by `testSecret`
options.why: Wrong: testSecret only verifies the AWSPENDING credential.

options.t: `AWSPENDING`, promoted by `setSecret`
options.why: Wrong: setSecret writes the new credential into the database, it does not move labels.

questions.explain: Four steps: createSecret, setSecret, testSecret, finishSecret.
questions.remember: New version = AWSPENDING until finishSecret moves AWSCURRENT to it. GetSecretValue returns AWSCURRENT by default.
variants: Need to roll back → move AWSCURRENT back with UpdateSecretVersionStage.
Which step tests the new credential → testSecret.
Which step changes the password in the DB → setSecret.

questions.q: A data account must read a secret owned by another AWS account. The secret is encrypted with the default `aws/secretsmanager` key. Which change makes cross-account access possible?

options.t: Add a resource policy only
options.why: Wrong: the other account still cannot use the AWS managed key to decrypt.

options.t: Re-encrypt with a customer managed KMS key, allow the other account in the key policy, and add a secret resource policy
options.why: Right: cross-account needs the resource policy, a CMK shared with the account, and IAM permissions on the caller side.

options.t: Copy the secret to Parameter Store standard
options.why: Wrong: standard parameters cannot be shared cross-account.

options.t: Enable replication to the other account's Region
options.why: Wrong: replication copies to Regions, not to access another account.

questions.explain: aws/secretsmanager cannot be shared; use a CMK.
questions.remember: Cross-account secret → resource policy + customer managed key shared to that account + caller's IAM policy allowing both secret and kms:Decrypt.
variants: Cross-account SecureString parameter → advanced tier shared via RAM, plus a shared CMK.
Same-account access → IAM policy and kms:Decrypt is enough.
Restrict to the organization → aws:PrincipalOrgID in the resource policy.

questions.q: A Lambda function reads the same secret thousands of times per second and gets throttled and runs up API costs. Which change helps most?

options.t: Request a higher GetSecretValue quota, since quotas are always adjustable
options.why: Wrong: most Secrets Manager quotas are not adjustable.

options.t: Cache the secret with the Secrets Manager caching component or the Parameters and Secrets Lambda Extension
options.why: Right: a local cache cuts API calls, cost, latency and throttling.

options.t: Replicate the secret to more Regions
options.why: Wrong: replicas are billed as extra secrets and do not reduce calls.

options.t: Move the value into a Lambda environment variable
options.why: Wrong: visible in configuration and no longer rotated.

questions.explain: Cache on the client; keep TTL short enough to survive rotation.
questions.remember: High read rate on a secret → cache client-side (caching components or Lambda extension, default TTL 300 s). Refresh on auth failure because rotation may change the value.
variants: Parameter Store throttling at default throughput → cache or enable higher throughput.
Reading many related values → store them in one JSON secret.
Cache too long after rotation → short TTL and retry on auth error.

questions.q: A pipeline stores 5,000 non-sensitive settings (endpoints, feature flags) read frequently. The team wants the lowest cost and a hierarchy such as `/prod/data/...`. Which service?

options.t: Secrets Manager, one secret per setting
options.why: Wrong: $0.40 per secret per month and per-call charges make this costly.

options.t: Parameter Store standard parameters, read with `GetParametersByPath`
options.why: Right: standard tier is free up to 10,000 parameters and offers a true hierarchy.

options.t: Parameter Store advanced parameters
options.why: Wrong: they are charged per parameter per month and are not needed here.

options.t: S3 objects encrypted with KMS
options.why: Wrong: no hierarchy API for config lookups and more code to maintain.

questions.explain: Plain config at volume and low cost: Parameter Store standard.
questions.remember: Many non-sensitive values, cost-sensitive, hierarchy → Parameter Store standard. Needs rotation, replication or managed DB integration → Secrets Manager.
variants: More than 10,000 parameters → advanced tier (100,000).
A few DB credentials that must rotate → Secrets Manager.
Gradual rollout and rollback of config → AppConfig.

questions.q: A 6 KB certificate chain must be stored as configuration, and another account must read it through AWS RAM sharing. Which option works?

options.t: Standard parameter
options.why: Wrong: limited to 4 KB and cannot be shared through RAM.

options.t: Advanced parameter
options.why: Right: 8 KB values and RAM sharing are advanced-tier features.

options.t: StringList parameter in the standard tier
options.why: Wrong: still a standard parameter with the 4 KB limit and no sharing.

options.t: Lambda environment variable
options.why: Wrong: not a shared store and not suitable for sharing cross-account.

questions.explain: Advanced tier: 8 KB, parameter policies, RAM sharing.
questions.remember: Value over 4 KB or cross-account sharing of a parameter → advanced tier (8 KB, RAM). Over 8 KB → Secrets Manager (64 KB) or S3 with a pointer.
variants: Value over 8 KB → Secrets Manager (up to 64 KB).
Alert before a parameter expires → advanced parameter with Expiration and ExpirationNotification policies.
Move advanced back to standard → not possible; recreate the parameter.

questions.q: Which statements about Secrets Manager versus Parameter Store are correct? Choose 2.

options.t: Secrets Manager supports built-in automatic rotation; Parameter Store does not
options.why: Right: rotation is a Secrets Manager feature; Parameter Store needs DIY Lambda/EventBridge.

options.t: Parameter Store standard parameters are free; Secrets Manager charges per secret and per API call
options.why: Right: $0.40 per secret per month plus $0.05 per 10,000 calls versus a free standard tier.

options.t: Parameter Store has built-in multi-Region replication
options.why: Wrong: replication is built into Secrets Manager; Parameter Store needs manual copying.

options.t: Secrets Manager values are limited to 4 KB
options.why: Wrong: the limit is 64 KB; 4 KB is the Parameter Store standard limit.

questions.explain: Rotation, replication and size favour Secrets Manager; cost and volume favour Parameter Store.
questions.remember: Secrets Manager: rotation, replication, resource policy, 64 KB, paid. Parameter Store: config and cheap secrets, hierarchy, free standard tier, no rotation.
variants: Which one offers parameter policies (expiration) → Parameter Store advanced.
Which one integrates managed secrets with RDS/Redshift → Secrets Manager.
One API to read both → /aws/reference/secretsmanager/<name> through Parameter Store.

questions.q: An ECS task needs a database password at start-up, and an engineer proposes putting it in the task definition environment as plain text. Which is the best alternative?

options.t: Keep the plain text value and restrict who can view the task definition
options.why: Wrong: the value is still exposed in configuration.

options.t: Reference the Secrets Manager secret (or a SecureString parameter) in the task definition `secrets` field
options.why: Right: ECS injects the value at start, so it never appears in the task definition.

options.t: Bake the password into the container image
options.why: Wrong: it leaks through the image and cannot be rotated.

options.t: Store the password in S3 without encryption
options.why: Wrong: insecure and adds code to fetch it.

questions.explain: Use the secrets field, not plain environment values.
questions.remember: Container credentials → task definition `secrets` pointing to Secrets Manager or Parameter Store. EKS equivalent is the Secrets Store CSI driver.
variants: EKS pods → Secrets Store CSI driver / ASCP.
CloudFormation templates → dynamic references {{resolve:secretsmanager:...}} or {{resolve:ssm-secure:...}}.
CodeBuild → environment variables of type PARAMETER_STORE or SECRETS_MANAGER.
